TRICKLE · V14 · STAGE 2 · 2 OCT 2026

Representing money

Fifteen ways to draw the same student month, tested on ten real scenarios. Explorations only. Tarun decides.

“1 dot = ₹100 is easy, but the problem comes with them combining into a line and a box. The biggest problem with not combining is larger amounts become harder to represent.”

“₹6,000, ₹600 for food, ₹500 for tea — all these numbers are too much.” — Tarun

The problem has three parts. Dots that merge into lines and boxes add a second and third shape to learn. Dots that never merge explode at ₹45,000 (450 marks, far past the ~20 a person can count at a glance; Kay 2016). Raw numbers everywhere are what students already tune out. Colour-coded categories add a key to memorise. What we keep: income splits into spending and savings, unspent money is saved, and progressive disclosure is how detail arrives.

Scenarios use the 6-month seed: ₹25 chai, ₹350 meal, ₹9,000 income (₹2,000 save, ₹7,000 spend), week ₹1,750 with ₹1,050 left, month ₹7,000 with ₹2,600 left, Food ₹2,800 · Travel ₹1,200 · Fun ₹1,000 · Study ₹600 · Subs ₹548, a ₹45,000 laptop goal, a ₹14,000 goal with ₹8,110 saved, four chais, and night spending. Filled = money still yours; outline = spent; dashed = not yet saved; ochre = savings.

Research behind the criteria. Kay et al. 2016: about 20 countable marks per glance; 100+ loses the benefit. Gigerenzer & Hoffrage 1995: counts (“3 of 10 days”) beat percentages, which hurts the waffle. Barrio 2016 / Riederer 2018: one perspective line in familiar units helps recall; small multipliers work best, so “≈ 1,800 chais” fails while “≈ 6 months of food” works. Olafsson & Pagel 2018 (ostrich effect): bad-news screens are avoided, so Home stays word-led. Garcia-Retamero 2010: show the whole, so spent stays as outlines. Neurath: repeat a unit, never enlarge it, which rules out gauges and big circles for big sums.

Top 4

S1 · Fixed dots, changing scale

  • Pro: one shape forever; dots never merge, which is Tarun’s concern.
  • Pro: every view stays under 20 marks; ₹45,000 = 9 dots of ₹5,000.
  • Con: the same dot means ₹100 or ₹1,000, so the unit must always be written.
  • Con: comparing week and month views needs the label.

S7 · Relative words

  • Pro: no number on Home; calmest (ostrich effect).
  • Pro: carries patterns (“nights cost more”).
  • Con: no proportion by itself; vague without a picture.
  • Con: weak friction at pay.

S8 · Label-first ranked bars

  • Pro: names on bars, so no colour key.
  • Pro: aligned lengths are the most accurate read (Cleveland & McGill).
  • Con: shows ₹, so it belongs in a tab, not Home.
  • Con: weak at ₹25.

S3 · Days of spending

  • Pro: uses Tarun’s “₹100–150 a day” finding; “5 days left” is felt.
  • Pro: scales: ₹45,000 ≈ 7½ months.
  • Con: depends on a “usual day” the student must accept.
  • Con: two meanings of “day” (calendar vs money).

Recommended hybrid (S15)

Home: one sentence in words (S7) over a week of ₹100 dots (S1): 17½ dots, filled = left, outline = spent. Under 20 marks; no ₹ figure. Pay moment: the dots the payment takes turn dashed before you confirm (friction, Soman 2001). Chai = ¼ dot; four chais fill one dot. Spending tab: label-first ranked bars by category (S8). Month dots switch to ₹1,000, with “1 dot = ₹1,000” written on screen. Savings / big goals: scaled dots (₹5,000) plus one days or months line (S3): “≈ 6 months of saving”. Detail: exact ₹, own equivalents (S12), and the hour strip for night spending (S11).

Why: dots never merge into lines or boxes, and large amounts are handled by stating the unit, not by new shapes. Words protect Home from the big number. Category names sit on the marks, so there is nothing to memorise. Rejected: gauges and waffles fail ₹45,000; notes, tallies and count labels lose honest proportion at scale.

Decisions for Tarun

D1 · How do big amounts stay drawable?

  1. Dot unit changes by view, written on screen (S1)
  2. ₹100 dots + count label (S2)
  3. Dots merge into tens (S14, v12)
  4. Convert to days/months (S3)

Suggested: A, with D as the perspective line.

D2 · What sits on Home at a glance?

  1. Words + week dots
  2. Words only
  3. Week dots only
  4. Weekly envelope

Suggested: A.

D3 · Home timeframe

  1. This week (₹1,750 = 17½ dots)
  2. This month (in ₹1,000 dots)
  3. Today (₹250 = 2½ dots)

Suggested: A. It matches weekly checkers and Yash’s mental limit.

D4 · How are categories shown without colour?

  1. Name on each bar, ranked
  2. Icon + name
  3. Colour + legend

Suggested: A or B.

D5 · Which perspective unit for big sums?

  1. Days/months of your spending
  2. Your own buys (chais, meals)
  3. Both by size (buys under ₹1,000, time above)
  4. None

Suggested: C.

D6 · Amounts under ₹100

  1. Partial dot (cup fill)
  2. Rounded, exact on tap

Suggested: A, so chai stays visible.

STAGE 2B · 2 OCT 2026

Coins and categories

Decided on 2 Oct: the dot is a coin (1 coin = ₹100, everywhere), Home is one sentence + this week’s coins with no ₹, and the timeframe is this week. Open: big amounts, and categories at 20+.

Run it with people: the coin test page randomises the top 2 coin variants and the top 2 category ideas, times each answer and gives a summary to paste back. Open the Trickle v14 coin test.

Part A · The coin and its count

D1 makes the dot a coin: 1 coin = ₹100 everywhere, never merged. Eight ways to show amounts past what you can count, on the same scenarios as Stage 2. Filled = still yours, outline = spent, dashed = not saved yet, ochre = savings, orange dashed = leaving with this payment.

V1

One coin ×N

“Past ten coins, one coin and a count.”

Smallest mark; but ×60 and ×6 look the same size, so the picture stops showing proportion past ten.

V2

Handful of 5 ×N

“Past ten, a handful of coins and the count.”

The handful says “a lot of coins” at once; still no proportion between ×26 and ×44.

V3

Row of 10 × rows

“Past twenty, one row of ten and how many rows.”

Re-introduces the “line” Tarun wants to avoid; “2.6 rows” is awkward.

V4

Draw up to 20, then handful ×N

“Up to 20 coins you see every one; past that, a handful and the count.”

Keeps a whole week (17½) fully drawn and countable (Kay 2016, ~20 marks); past 20 the handful + count takes over. Five is at the edge of instant counting.

V5

Coin with count badge

“A coin with a number on it is that many coins.”

Compact, but a badge reads as a notification count, not money.

V6

Handful + ₹ wording

“Past ten, a few coins and the rupee amount.”

Clear but puts a ₹ figure on the glance, which D2 rules out for Home.

V7

Handful ×N, ₹ underneath

“The count is coins; the small line is rupees.”

Good for tabs and detail: count leads, rupees underneath for people who think in ₹.

V8

Coin pile (side view)

“A pile of coins, with how many are in it.”

Most coin-like and tactile, but overlapping coins are a merge in disguise and are hard to count.

STUDY

A payment takes coins out

“Before you confirm, the coins this payment takes lift out of your week.”

₹350 is 3½ coins. On the pay screen those coins turn orange-dashed and slide out of the row before the confirm button; after paying they become outlines. This is the friction moment from Stage 0 (Soman 2001: rehearsing the cost at payment), without a ₹ figure.

STUDY

Coin rendering and partial coins

Flat, rim, or rim + shine; a part-coin as a cup fill or a cut wedge (like a quarter of a coin).

Suggested: rim, no shine. The inner ring makes a dot read as a coin at 14px and survives black & white (try the toggle above); shine adds noise at small sizes. For part-coins the wedge reads as “a piece of a coin” and matches a quarter; the cup fill reads better as filling up over four chais. Both are in the test.

STUDY

Week, month and goal with the same coin

Same coin, same ₹100; the frame and the word change, never the unit.

A week is drawn coin by coin (it fits under 20). A month and a goal switch to the handful + count. The switch itself tells you “this is a big amount” without a new shape. Savings stay ochre everywhere, so a goal never looks like spending.

1 · V4 Draw up to 20, then handful ×N

  • A whole week (17½ coins) is always fully drawn, so Home never shows a count, only coins.
  • 20 is the countable limit from Kay et al. 2016; 5 sits at the edge of instant counting (Kaufman 1949).
  • Past 20 the handful says “many coins” and ×N gives the exact count in the same unit (Neurath: repeat, don’t enlarge).
  • Con: between 21 and ~60 the picture does not show proportion; the count carries it.

2 · V1 One coin ×N

  • Smallest and calmest; works inside list rows and category lines.
  • Pure count format, which people read well (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage 1995).
  • Con: ×11 and ×450 look identical at a glance; it relies fully on reading the number.
  • Test question: does the handful in V4 actually help, or is the count doing all the work?

Scales 4 · Consistent with coins 4 · Learnable 3 · Custom-friendly 4

1 · B1 Name-first ranked rows (+ B3 emoji, + B4 on Home)

  • The name is what the user typed, so a custom “Bike EMI” is as clear as “Food”; no key to learn.
  • Ranked by size, rows aligned on one edge: aligned length is the most accurate comparison (Cleveland & McGill 1984).
  • The user’s own emoji can sit before the name as a quick anchor, never instead of it.
  • On Home, only the top 4 + Others (B4); the full list on tap. Coins look the same in every row.

2 · B5 Families: Needs / Wants / Fixed

  • Three groups stay learnable at any count; 20 categories become 3 lines at a glance.
  • Matches how students already talk (Harsh: knowing where he wants to spend; Nishad: purpose accounts) and income = spending + savings.
  • Fixed (EMI, Subs, Phone, Gym) can carry the “takes money in 2 days” reminder.
  • Con: someone has to place each custom category; ambiguous ones (Chai: Need or Want?) need a default.

Not recommended as the identity: monograms (B2) collide (“Gi” Gifts vs “Gy” Gym), dynamic colour (B6) is a nice accent but not an identity, coin rows (B7) get too long past ₹3,000, and search (B8) belongs on the full list, not the glance. Merchant grouping (B9) is a setup aid: it proposes categories from UPI merchants so people rarely make them by hand.

Decisions for Tarun (Stage 2b)

E1 · How does a big amount look?

  1. V4: draw up to 20 coins, then a handful of 5 + ×N
  2. V1: one coin + ×N past 10
  3. V7: handful ×N with ₹ underneath (tabs only)

Suggested: run the coin test, then pick A or B; use C in tabs and detail either way.

E2 · Coin rendering and part-coins

  1. Rim, cup fill
  2. Rim, wedge
  3. Flat, cup fill

Suggested: A or B (the test page uses rim + cup fill; add wedge if you want to compare).

E3 · Category identity

  1. Name-first ranked rows, own emoji optional, top 4 + Others on Home
  2. Families (Needs / Wants / Fixed) with categories inside
  3. Both: families on Home, name-first rows inside each family

Suggested: test A vs B; C is the likely end state if families test well.

E4 · Should colour carry anything for categories?

  1. No colour at all
  2. Colour only for this week’s top 3

Suggested: A until the test shows a need.

E5 · Who places a custom category in a family?

  1. User picks on creation
  2. Trickle suggests from the merchant, user confirms

Suggested: B (matches “take it from my GPay”).
